articles.title: Nolan Wells' friends open up about Christian faith journey after Horn Island death
articles.summary: Nolan Wells' closest friends reveal how the Mississippi teen's death on Horn Island transformed their Christian faith in an exclusive interview.
articles.body: The death of Mississippi teen Nolan Wells has left his closest friends grieving and searching for answers, but they say the loss has also deepened their faith and brought them closer to God. "I learned to lean on the Lord," Warren Hudson, one of Wells' friends, told Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany in an exclusive interview. "I know my friends did as well. And I know that's what Nolan would want me to do." Another friend, Jax Pitalo, described Wells' death as a turning point for the group. "Right after the first three days or so, I was like, if this did anything, it got us all closer to God," Pitalo said. Wells, 18, disappeared July 4 after taking a boat trip with a group of friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. Search crews combed the area for two days before a National Park Service ranger discovered his body at the island's northwestern tip on July 6. MISSISSIPPI GRAND JURY DECLINES TO INDICT ANYONE IN DEATH OF 18-YEAR-OLD WHO VANISHED IN COASTAL WATERS Months later, a Jackson County, Mississippi, grand jury returned a "no true bill" in Wells' death investigation, declining to indict anyone after finding insufficient evidence of criminal wrongdoing. The grand jury found his death was consistent with drowning. But for the friends who knew Wells long before his death became the subject of headlines and online speculation, the months since have been about grieving someone they loved while leaning more deeply into their Christian faith. "We started going to church more," Morgan Seymour, a third friend, told McEnany. "Everything from that moment on was like for God, for Jesus," he continued, prompting Hudson to add, "For Nolan." McEnany said the young men have faced intense online scrutiny and accusations in the months since Wells' death, even as they attempted to process the loss. GOVERNOR BLAMES ACTIVISTS IN NOLAN WELLS CASE FOR ‘STOKING DIVISION,’ OFFICIAL SAYS FBI PROBING THREATS "These young men, unfortunately, were demonized and dragged through a lot, and they loved Nolan," McEnany told "Fox & Friends Weekend," noting that one had been friends with Wells since elementary school. The scrutiny intensified as theories about Wells' disappearance spread online, including unsubstantiated claims that his friends were responsible for his death and that the incident was racially motivated. Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath said, however, that the grand jury found "absolutely no evidence" to support allegations that Wells' death was motivated by race. "Nolan's friends loved Nolan and Nolan loved them," McIlrath said following the grand jury's decision. "Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that." Wells' family and civil rights attorney Ben Crump have challenged the grand jury's decision, pointing to bruising and blunt-force injuries described by the family's independent pathologist and calling for further investigation into how he died, including an independent federal review by the Justice Department. Fox News' Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

articles.title: Shropshire Astronomical Society get permission for observatory
articles.summary: The Shropshire Astronomical Society plans to install the dome at Rodington village hall.
articles.body:
A group of amateur astronomers have been given permission to set up a mini-observatory at a village hall.

Members of the Shropshire Astronomical Society (SAS) now plan to transfer over the out of use dome and telescope once used by the Irish Rangers at the Tern Hill army base near Market Drayton.

They have been based at Rodington Village Hall, near Shrewsbury, for 25 years but think the telescope will raise interest in astronomy.

In granting permission, Telford and Wrekin planners said the curved gloss white fibreglass dome used to house the telescope would be "somewhat unusual" but would add "some visual interest to the site.

In the group's application, the society's Stephen Szwajkun wrote: "It will be a first public astronomical observatory in the area and provide inspiration for the diverse residents of Telford and Wrekin as well as the wider area."

Society chairman Philip Osman said a permanent observatory would encourage participation and also give the group the opportunity to organise community outreach activities.

"The dome will be the only publicly accessible observatory in the county and we hope that this new facility will allow us to broaden our outreach activities and successfully engage with a new generation," he said.

Osman also said an agreement had been reached to purchase the mini observatory in May.

The domed structure is set to be a little less than 2.7m (8ft 9inches) tall and council officials were satisfied that the proposal would not result in unacceptable noise, disturbance or any other disruption for nearby residents.

They added that it was "not considered likely to result in a significant increase in traffic or parking demand".

Planners agreed that it would provide a useful additional community and educational facility.

This news was gathered by the Local Democracy Reporting Service which covers councils and other public service organisations.

articles.title: Book's claim that Hebrew punctuation is a relic of brutal colonial system sparks criticism
articles.summary: The New Yorker faces backlash for reviewing a book that links Hebrew punctuation to colonialism and the history of Jewish migration to Israel.
articles.body: The New Yorker drew criticism from several commentators online after publishing a review of a new book whose author links Hebrew punctuation to colonialism and the history of Jewish migration to Israel. The book, titled "On the Mark: From Periods to Interrobangs, How Punctuation Remade the World" and written by author Florence Hazrat, is drawing scrutiny after the New Yorker's Louis Menand highlighted its claim that punctuation marks in the Hebrew language are "relics" of a "brutal colonial system." The review written by Menand describes Hazrat's book as "irreverent and delightfully intellectual," but says its premise — that the "history of punctuation is the history of humanity" — leads to "overreach." FAMILY MEMBER OF LAWYER WHO COINED 'GENOCIDE' SEEKS TO STRIP NAME FROM GROUP ACCUSING ISRAEL OF ATROCITY "Today this brutal oppression (aided and abetted by the United States, Germany, and a host of other countries through arms deliveries, technological support, and trade deals) has evolved into the worst crime of all crimes: genocide," Hazrat wrote. Hazrat goes on to argue in her book that adding punctuation helped turn Hebrew from a written language into a spoken one. CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS She argues that the introduction of punctuation into the language is "paving the way for an artificial sense of unity among Jewish people from all over the globe, encouraging them to move to the land that already had people—a people made to suffer and bear the brunt of European antisemitism in the most horrendous ways for generations." While Menand takes issue with Hazrat's stance on the topic in his review, writing that "It seems (the reason is not altogether clear) that, had Yiddish been the official language of Israel, atrocities might have been avoided," the New Yorker's decision to publish the review prompted criticism from several commentators online. JEWISH EDUCATORS FACE RAMPANT ANTISEMITISM IN TEACHERS UNIONS, NEW REPORT FINDS In an X post, deputy editor of Jewish News UK Daniel Sugarman, blasted the argument, writing, "The author of this book is, predictably, an academic in the UK and a ‘BBC New Generation Thinker.’" "Seems like the new generation has the same thoughts as older generations when it comes to pseudoscientific crap roping in Jews," he continued. THE NEW YORKER CLAIMS WOMEN CAN BE 'KIND OF PREGNANT' IN ARTICLE QUESTIONING PREGNANCY TESTS Isaac de Castro, audience editor of Tablet Magazine, also took to social media to weigh in, writing in an X post that "We’re at the ‘Hebrew punctuation is a colonialist tool to oppress Palestinians, the real victims of European antisemitism, and assemble a worldwide cabal of Jews, previously completely unaffiliated’ stage of mass psychosis." In another post to X, a user said they would cancel their New Yorker subscription, adding the publication "should never have published this." Fox News Digital reached out to Hazrat and the New Yorker for comment. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg, an outspoken Jewish voice, also denounced the claims, telling Fox News Digital that "blaming commas and question marks for regional conflict shows just how deeply antisemitism rots basic critical thinking." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The attempt to demonize Hebrew down to its punctuation isn’t serious linguistics. It is an obsessive crusade to deny the Jewish people our history, language, and humanity," Aronberg said. "There is no issue too absurd, and apparently no punctuation mark too small, for modern anti-Israel activists to twist into an indictment against the Jewish state."

articles.title: Remains of Bulgaria’s Czar Samuel return ‘home’ after 1,000 years
articles.summary: The emperor is a symbol of Bulgarian national identity whose repatriation stoked tensions with Greece.
articles.body:
More than 1,000 years after his death, the remains of medieval ruler Czar Samuel have arrived in Bulgaria.

A symbol of Bulgarian national identity, Samuel was a warrior emperor who battled the Byzantine Empire to expand his kingdom before suffering defeat and dying soon after in 1014. His supposed remains were discovered in a Greek border area in the 1960s.

The coffin and remains were flown on Saturday to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on board a military aircraft that was surrounded by air force fighter jets.

Thousands of people poured into a public square to honour the czar’s arrival, which capped years of fraught negotiations between Bulgaria and Greece until an accord was reached this week.

Bulgarian politicians across the spectrum paid tribute to the medieval ruler, listening to the national anthem and a 21-gun salute.

“Today, we Europeans are learning to read history with a desire to belong not only to our homeland, but also to the culture that unites us across the entire European continent,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.

“That is why Europe must not reopen old wounds but must work for peace as the supreme good,” Radev continued, referring to the centuries-old rivalry between neighbouring Greece and Bulgaria.

Crowds cheered as fighter jets performed a flypast.

Martin Nestorov, a 42-year-old software engineer, told the AFP news agency he attended the ceremony “to welcome Czar Samuel back to Bulgaria, where he belongs”.

“I am here because I am Bulgarian, and a Bulgarian is returning to his homeland,” added Tsanka Zlatkova, 65, a retired art historian.

A procession brought the remains to be laid in the Church of Saint Sofia, a sixth-century basilica that is the capital’s namesake and where church officials say Samuel was baptised.

The handover of Samuel’s remains is part of a broader accord between the Greek and Bulgarian culture ministers.

In exchange, Greece is slated to receive 48 objects that Bulgarian troops pillaged from churches and monasteries in Greece during World War I.

Speaking before the handover, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said he hoped the ceremony would boost Greece’s campaign to repatriate the Parthenon Marbles , a collection of 2,500-year-old marble sculptures taken from the Acropolis in Athens and later displayed in the British Museum.

“The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” Mitsotakis said, adding that historical heirlooms “cannot be treated as the spoils of war”.

Bulgaria is not the only country to have claims on Samuel. A huge statue of the czar stands in the North Macedonian capital of Skopje, with Macedonians claiming him as “their” ruler.

In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended presenting Samuel as the head of a state that “most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire”, based in what is currently North Macedonia.

articles.title: In 2011, Tony Stewart built a nearly 20,000-sq-ft home on 415 Indiana acres with a waterfall, 8,700-gallon aquarium and bowling alley; after asking $30 million, it is now listed at $18.9 million
articles.summary: In 2011, NASCAR champion Tony Stewart completed a nearly 20,000-square-foot home on 415 acres in Columbus, Indiana.
articles.body: In 2011, NASCAR champion Tony Stewart completed a nearly 20,000-square-foot home on 415 acres in Columbus, Indiana. The property, known as Hidden Hollow Ranch, was built as a private retreat with a stocked lake, wildlife, indoor entertainment spaces and features designed to bring the outdoors into the house. It is now listed for $18.9 million.According to Realtor.com, the ranch has changed its asking price several times since it was first put on the market. Stewart listed the property for $30 million in 2022. In 2024, it returned to the market at $22.5 million, a $7.5 million reduction from the earlier asking price. The property website now lists the ranch at $18.9 million.Stewart bought the land in 2004 and later built the main house, which measures 19,713 square feet, according to the property's official website. The ranch has six bedrooms and eight full bathrooms and three half bathrooms. It also includes a 3,500-square-foot guest house, a six-car garage and an accessory building with workshops, storage and a full bathroom.The property was designed around both the wooded land and the activities available on it. Its 415 acres include a nine-acre stocked lake and a licensed hunting preserve. The main house also has several unusual features, including a two-story waterfall, a 1,500-gallon koi stream and an 8,700-gallon freshwater aquarium.A home built around the outdoorsThe house was constructed using lodgepole pine sourced from the Northern Rockies. The property website says the flooring includes white oak and red oak hardwood from New York, along with stone from Texas. Indiana bedrock was used for fireplaces in the breakfast room, great room and screened-in porch.One of the most noticeable features is in the entrance. A 1,500-gallon stream stocked with koi runs through the entryway and has a bridge over it. The stream connects with a two-story waterfall, making water a central feature of the home's interior.The great room has an 8,700-gallon freshwater aquarium. The official property website also lists a cleaning room and tank for the fish. A large television is built into the room, while the space also includes a fireplace and views towards the private lake.The kitchen has a hibachi grill with commercial exhaust, a Wolf range and a Sub-Zero refrigerator. The property website lists hickory and knotty alder kitchen cabinets, along with heated floors throughout the house.The main level also has a master suite with a kitchenette, walk-in shower, rain shower and jacuzzi. TVs are built into the mirrors. There are two laundry rooms in the house.The upper level has four bedrooms, all with en-suite bathrooms and views of the surrounding property.Bowling alley, golf simulator and onyx barThe lower level is designed around recreation. It includes a two-lane bowling alley, a billiards room, a workout room with a full bathroom and a golf simulator room.There is also a lighted onyx bar and other entertainment space. Earlier Realtor.com coverage described the lower level as having a bowling alley, game area, golf simulator room, gym and bar.The house also has several custom-made fixtures. The official property website says the entry fixture was made in Alaska, while all the light fixtures were custom made in Utah. A ring from a naval battleship is used to hold the great room roof in place.The property also includes three geothermal heat systems, two 1,000-gallon commercial-grade water heaters and a Cummins generator. Its roof has three layers, with corrugated steel shingles on top, along with custom-made copper gutters and downspouts.415 acres with a stocked lakeThe land surrounding the house is a major part of Hidden Hollow Ranch. It includes a nine-acre stocked lake with largemouth bass, bluegill, carp, gar, perch and crappie.The ranch is also a licensed hunting preserve. The official property website lists 15 elk, 300 deer and turkey on the property. Realtor.com previously reported that the wooded acreage included elk, deer and turkey and described the lake as stocked for fishing.The property is also zoned for a bed and breakfast, giving the ranch another permitted use.When Stewart first listed the ranch in 2022, he described it as his dream home. “This is truly my dream home,” Stewart said in a statement at the time. “We enjoyed every square inch of the land here. This became my place to get away and relax with my family and friends.”He also spoke about the range of activities available on the property, saying, “The land is great for hunting and fishing, off-roading, or just sitting on the porch and enjoying the stars at night. It is the perfect blend of entertainment and relaxation.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.body: An Indian woman with US Green Card shared the experience of a B1/B2 visa interview at Mumbai Consulate attended by her mother which ended in a flat refusal. As the woman shared her mother's interview experience, seeking advice on what they did wrong, it emerged as an interesting case to study for B1/B2 visa applicants, as the denial rates in India are quite high. Whenever visa officers don't find strong ties of the applicants with India, they deny visa detecting "immigration intent" which means that they suspect that the applicants may not return to India.In this case, as specified by the Reddit post, the visa officer asked the mother, a widow staying in India with her son while the daughter is a US Green Card holder with a US citizen spouse, the purpose of her visit. The mother had no history of international travel and it was her first intended trip to the US to attend the housewarming ceremony of the daughter.The trip was planned for a month. The visa officer asked her about the funding of the trip. The mother, a widowed housewife, said she was funding the trip herself through savings. "I have my savings good enough to cover my one month trip. I live with my son so he takes care of my expenses and I also survive out of the interest from my FD and other investments. I also do some small embroidery work but it's seasonal and not often available," the mother said."They didn't ask for any documents. my mother has property and all the investments on her name. I don't know what went wrong here," the Redditor said. Within five minutes of this conversation, the visa was denied. The visa officer also told her to apply again.What went wrong?Redditors pointed out that though a similar case may get approved in another consulate or by a different visa officer, the mother did not actually show any strong ties to India. articles.title: Drug addicts turn to painkillers amid Nasha Mukt crackdown in J&K
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Drug users and peddlers in Jammu & Kashmir are increasingly turning to pharmaceutical opioids, primarily painkillers, amid an intensified
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Drug users and peddlers in Jammu & Kashmir are increasingly turning to pharmaceutical opioids, primarily painkillers, amid an intensified crackdown under Nasha Mukt Abhiyaan to make the UT “narcotics-free”.“It seems they were mixing several painkiller drugs to get the effect of heroin,” a police officer said, adding that abusers frequently use prescription medicines like Tramadol and Tapentadol, which they refer to as “Tapal“ in their local slang.Investigations have so far led to the recovery of 2,19,425 tablets and capsules of pharmaceutical drugs, as well as 3.830 kg of codeine-containing liquid, including the storage containers, police said.Since its launch on April 11, Nasha Mukt Abhiyaan has resulted in over 4,000 arrests, the seizure of 288 properties, and registration of 3,257 cases under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. The campaign includes awareness programmes, the destruction of illicit poppy crops, and random urine drug testing for drivers.On Thursday, Srinagar police arrested eight people after busting a major network involved in the procurement, transportation, storage, distribution, and financing of banned pharmaceutical products, with supply lines extending well beyond J&K.Among those arrested was Haris Hameed Malla, a Srinagar resident identified as a key accused in the network allegedly headed by Waseem Ahmad Zargar. While Zargar claimed to operate a legitimate pharmaceutical business, Malla allegedly projected himself as an influential figure, frequently flaunting photographs with top police and civil officials.His Instagram account featured photographs with Union ministers Nitin Gadkari and Chirag Paswan, as well as Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and National Conference MP Aga Ruhullah Mehdi. On his social media profiles, Malla described himself as the editor-in-chief of the “India News Panel” and a community journalist. Malla had also posted a letter on X, purportedly written by L-G Manoj Sinha, regarding the UT’s efforts to combat drug abuse.A police officer said Zargar, the alleged primary supplier, revealed details of the operation during questioning. Malla subsequently fled the Valley but was traced to Bengaluru, where he was arrested.As part of the ongoing case, a house and two vehicles were attached in Srinagar’s Old City. Officials noted that the case is highly significant as locals are increasingly coming forward to report the growing drug menace. articles.title: 100 detained as protesters return to demand CEC’s removal
articles.summary: Around 150 protesters demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s removal over alleged SIR electoral roll irregularities were detained near Jantar Mantar in Delhi.
articles.body: New Delhi: Around 150 people demanding chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s removal were detained in and around Jantar Mantar Saturday. Security forces were deployed at various entry and exit points of Jantar Mantar to prevent people from mobilising for demonstrations called by student and political outfits.Those detained included senior advocates Prashant Bhushan and Kapil Sibal, Swaraj India founder Yogendra Yadav and AISA national president Neha Bora. Bhushan and Yadav continued their protest inside Bahadurgarh police station and livestreamed a session on social media, explaining their demands.A day after Friday’s protest on the same issue, participants again demanded Kumar’s removal due to alleged irregularities in Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. In Delhi, the names of over 47 lakh people have been deleted in the draft SIR roll and another 33 lakh have received notices to explain “logical discrepancies” in their records.“The booth-level officers are now asking me to register as a new voter using Form 6 instead of updating my new address. After 40 years of living in Delhi and voting in every election, why should I do that?” asked Diwakar, who stood away from protesters to avoid detention.Over 50 buses were parked at various points near Jantar Mantar to detain the protesting students. At 1.43pm, a few sloganeering students were picked up and shoved into buses; a string of detentions followed. “If there’s enough of a crowd to cause trouble, detentions are warranted. But they’ve planned to take us away as soon as we arrive to prevent even a small gathering,” said a Delhi University student.Around 3pm, members of All India Students’ Association marched from Rafi Marg to Janpath Marg and tried to breach the barricades leading towards Jantar Mantar, triggering a tussle between students and police. “We’ll definitely be detained,” said Altaf Husain of All India Students’ Federation. “But it is important to register our protest against the injustices committed by the authorities. We won’t back down even in the face of repression,” he reiterated.Many participants were, however, unhappy with the way the protest was organised. Although scheduled to begin at 1pm, it gained momentum only by 3pm, and those who gathered were confused about how to enter the protest site as police barricades were set up at all points, they said. “There is no leadership for this protest. Even with internet access, we don’t know where to go and how to get there,” said Atrey, a DU student.A statement released by AISA alleged manhandling, including groping, of women protesters, journalists and lawyers by male police personnel. A video circulating on social media showed a male police officer grabbing AISA national president Bora from behind to detain her. Protesters immediately surrounded the officer, compelling him to release her. articles.title: Trump ramps up pressure on US Republicans to end US clock switching
articles.summary: The US president published a lawmaker’s cell phone number as he called for the passage of a bill making DST permanent.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has increased the pressure on US Senate Republicans to make Daylight Saving Time permanent, singling out one of the body’s members for stalling legislation to end the twice-a-year changing of clocks.

In a social media post on Saturday, Trump blasted US Senator Tom Cotton for “holding up” the Sunshine Protection Act, which Trump has personally opted to call the “No More Changing of Clocks Act”.

“For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social account about the Arkansas Republican. “It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion”.

“Nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year and, having sunshine in the afternoon is better than early in the morning!” he added.

Trump went even further, publishing what he claimed was Cotton’s phone number as he implored Arkansas residents to pressure him. The move echoed a moment during the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, when then-candidate Trump gave out US Senator Lindsey Graham’s number after the former rival criticised him.

Al Jazeera called the number listed in Trump’s post, but an automated message stated the voicemail box was full. Cotton’s spokesperson and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

The president has routinely pushed Senate Republicans to pass legislation mandating year-round daylight saving, which would end Americans’ decades-long practice of changing their clocks twice a year to increase daylight hours. On Friday, Trump urged the US Senate to approve the bill, which passed the US House in July by a 308-117 vote.

Cotton has previously opposed the bill, arguing in a US Senate floor speech last year that farmers, construction workers, commuters and children heading to school would begin their days in the dark during the winter.

Trump disputed that argument in a separate post on Saturday, saying the bill “would be a very nice and easy WIN for the Republican Party”.

“If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, workplaces, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so”, Trump wrote.

Trump, an avid golfer, also highlighted what he considered to be another selling point of the bill: the North American Professional Golfers’ Association (PGA) tour.

“The PGA TOUR, as an example, needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments”, he wrote in a post, which included a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp supporting the bill. “Likewise, regular Golfers, Tennis Players, Hunters and, perhaps more importantly, Farmers who want more Daylight to play or work.”

The US president, who spent part of Saturday at his golf club in Sterling, Virginia, indicated in a subsequent post that he had received personal feedback on the proposal: “I don’t know about anyone else, but a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it’s DARK. It’s depressing!”

In 1974, the US Congress briefly adopted year-round daylight saving time in response to the country’s energy crisis. But Congress repealed the law less than a year later over safety concerns as children commuted to school before sunrise.

US senators left Washington this week and have no set plans to return until after the November 3 midterm elections.

Some members, such as Senator John Kennedy, weren’t optimistic that Senate Republican Leader John Thune would bring the bill up for a vote before polling day.

“It’s dead as disco,” the Louisiana Republican told Reuters this week of Trump’s push to make daylight saving time permanent. “My sense is it would have trouble passing … I don’t think the leader is going to bring it up.”

articles.title: Garth Stein bought a 1924 Seattle house in 2001 and spent 25 years restoring and updating it while raising three children; with the family now downsizing, the 3,970-sq-ft ‘forever house’ is asking $2.45 million
articles.summary: Bestselling author Garth Stein has listed his ‘forever house’ in Seattle.
articles.body: Bestselling author Garth Stein has listed his ‘forever house’ in Seattle. Stein is best known for his 2008 bestseller The Art of Racing in the Rain, which was adapted into a film in 2019. Seven years before the fame, Stein and his wife, filmmaker Andrea Perlbinder Stein, bought this Seattle home, and now it’s back on the market. The brick Colonial Revival in Seattle’s Mount Baker neighbourhood is asking $2,450,000, Realtor.com reports. Amy Sajer of Windermere Real Estate/Luxury Portfolio International is handling the sale.A forever house in SeattleStein and his wife bought the place in 2001, seven years before the novel came out. They called it their forever house. They wanted to raise their kids there. Three kids later, the youngest has gone to college, and the couple is ready to downsize.“They were there 25 years. Their last kid has gone to college. It’s time to focus their energy elsewhere. Garth said, ‘We always considered this our forever house, and we made our decisions about the renovations accordingly.’ You really feel that when you’re in the house,” Amy Sajer, the listing agent, said.The house was originally built in the 1920sThe Stein family’s Seattle house has more history than they could remember. The house was built in 1924. The Steins started improving the brick Colonial home almost at once and never really stopped.“The improvements started right away, in 2001, and they have done things all along their ownership. They’ve always maintained it and did whatever they needed to update it,” Sajer told the outlet.In 2009, the couple gave the home a major renovation. Rocky Rochon reworked the traditional layout to let in light and open up sightlines. The home’s original character survived, including a Batchelder tile fireplace in the living room. The new additions they made were air conditioning and all-new bathrooms. The house spans 3,970 sq ft and has four bedrooms and 3.5 bathrooms. All the bedrooms are located in the corners of the home, providing privacy as well as breathtaking views. The primary suite has a lake view and a sunroom. There is a lower-level space that can be used as an office, guest room or creative studio.Two of the bathrooms, designed by Marianne Simon Design in marble, glass and brass, won a Luxe Design Award in 2018. The kitchen has a Viking range, two sinks, custom cabinetry and countertops in both marble and butcher block.Steel-and-glass French doors in the living and dining rooms open onto bluestone terraces. Outside, there is a gas firepit and a built-in kitchen. There is also a detached two-car garage.According to the agent, it is a house that has been fully redone without announcing it. “It’s an old house with soul, and you’ve got these wonderful materials, but literally everything’s been done and you don’t necessarily see that,” says Sajer. “It’s all new, but it doesn’t scream ‘new’, and it has all this warmth.”The lake is a block away. Mount Baker itself was laid out by the Olmsted brothers, and the street plan still follows the land.“Mount Baker was laid out by the Olmsted brothers ... according to the topography of the area. You see these beautiful curved streets that take in the view and the gracious surroundings. Lake Park Drive runs through Mount Baker Park. You have trails, tennis courts and a playground, and it spills right into the lakefront,” the agent told the outlet.The house has no historical designation. But this neighbourhood draws buyers who care about preserving old architecture anyway, and here the hard part is finished.“People really want to be in these older established neighbourhoods where you have the wonderful architecture and the brick legacy, but not everyone wants to redo the plumbing and the electrical. This house did all that,” Sajer explains.Mount Baker is often in high demand, as homes here rarely come up for sale. Sajer has seen it through her career. “I sell a lot in that neighbourhood. All of my sellers have been there either 30, 40, or 60 years. It’s that vibe of a neighbourhood where people stay forever.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: AI models could harm young people's body image, warn experts
articles.summary: Could the rise of AI models in advertising and on social media harm young people's body confidence?
articles.body:
AI models are popping up more and more across social media and advertising, but how might this affect body image?

Mia Perumal, who has recovered from an eating disorder, said she's worried the technology could make unrealistic beauty standards even harder for young people to escape.

The 19-year-old Cardiff University student said she believes if she'd had access to AI during her eating disorder, it would have had a "terrible impact".

AI-generated videos and photos are getting harder to spot too, she said.

This story contains material about eating disorders and self-harm.

When Mia Perumal was 12 she says she was fed harmful content via social media algorithms.

Now she fears the rise of AI models is magnifying the damage on other young people.

Mia has noticed an increase in very thin AI beautiful people on social media in the past year, the comments often being from 12-year-old girls saying: "Dream body, drop your workout routine I want to look like this."

She said she finds it "really sad" because looking like AI models is completely unobtainable, she believes the only option to prevent harm is for AI to be controlled.

Mia said: "It's all very well saying 'oh, it's AI, it's not real,' But eating disorders don't really listen to rationality."

She said she wants young people to "be cautious, question everything".

In the early 2000s Kelly Watts, like most teenagers, was worried about the way she looked and said she was constantly comparing herself to people around her and models in magazines, she said.

Now 41, she is worried her 11-year-old son will compare his body to fake photographs of "perfect people".

As a freelancer in marketing, AI in business images are something Kelly is seeing everywhere, but often without tags meaning it is hard to determine whether it is real or fake.

"At first, I didn't realise they were AI, but the more you see it, the more you can't unsee it. Now, I see it on quite a regular basis," said Kelly.

Her son Oscar loves playing rugby and is becoming more aware that "some friends are taller", she said.

While he has not raised concerns about his body, she fears he could look up to AI characters online.

The 11-year-old watches YouTube and does not yet have social media. But this does not keep him away from AI, which she fears has infiltrated YouTube's content.

Watching footballers who have six-packs is already a body-image influence, she said, let alone being then shown AI generated people who are unrealistic.

"Especially with children, it's going to be 'can they ever get to that point?

"It's putting a lot of pressure on them, which they don't need," she said. "No one and nothing is perfect. I don't want him growing up thinking he has to be perfect."

"I'm his mum, and the last person he's going to listen to over a big influencer," she said, even if that influencer is AI.

Kelly said AI-literacy is important, and being able to spot real vs fake is essential.

"At what point do we need to be aware that it potentially can be damaging to us and our children, and AI should definitely be labelled more."

"Why do we want to compare ourselves to a robot instead of a human?"

"As human beings, we have this tendency to compare ourselves to others," said Phillippa Diedrichs, professor of psychology at the Centre for Appearance Research, UWE Bristol.

She said: "If we're comparing ourselves to a very narrow beauty standard, which typically tends to be the case, the beauty ideals that we have are very narrowly defined, and that inevitably means that many of us are not going to meet those beauty ideals.

"This is particularly the case with social media and digitally constructed images because they don't even exist in biological reality.

"We compare ourselves and when we fall short, this can lead us to doubt ourselves and feel negatively about our own appearance."

She said if AI was used to create more diversity and inclusion, then "when we compare ourselves, we feel alike and similar, which can either have a neutral or positive impact on our wellbeing".

Diedrichs said unless the designers prompt AI to show realistic or diverse features, "it's going to give you an image that defaults to the average" data set of the "narrow" traditional beauty standards.

"So for example, people of colour, gender, queer people, people with kind of interesting and distinguishing facial features, it means that they're going to be left out," she said.

"You can try and overcompensate that with the way you prompt and create these images. But if you don't do that, you're going to get very generic images, which tend to reinforce a lot of the biases that we have in society."

She said it could create even more unrealistic beauty standards, "if it's not done carefully or with some thought because it will default to the average of whatever it's learnt from.

Diedrichs said there are "tell-tale" signs like "the texture of the skin or the eyes" and how "coily hair" looks.

She added that the absence of blemishes or pores can be a good way of identifying AI, however it is constantly getting better.

Diedrichs said teenagers can be influenced but they are also often "critical and aware, and have more knowledge about technology than older people".

"The thing is, though, we can be aware that these things are happening, but it doesn't necessarily stop us from wanting to look like those images," she said.

She said she recommended asking if the images or advertising is "serving you, does that make you feel good about yourself? Does it make you feel inspired, lit up?"

"If it's making you feel lacking, that's a really important signal to pay attention to, and suggests that maybe this isn't for me to be looking at."

Diedrichs said AI models in advertising could enable small brands to have a large number of diverse models, or global brands to advertise in multiple markets.

"There could be these benefits for diversity," she said.

However, she noted the "knock on effect to creative industries and people working in this space. I would never like to see AI completely replace" the artistry and creativity of humans.

"As a consumer, you have a lot of power as well. You can express your views on this in the comment section," she said. "Brands will see."

Zoe Lee and Hannah Marriott, researchers at Cardiff Business School said AI-generation fashion models and digital twins, virtual replicas of real models are becoming more common.

Brands such as Balmain, Levi's and H&M have experimented with the technology, they said.

But Lee and Marriott's research has found that consumers often reacted negatively to AI-generated models once they realised they were not real.

In focus groups, participants told them they would "rather have a real person and way less people representing us, but they be real", arguing AI models could never reflect lived experience.

Marriott said they also found people would "emotionally detach themselves" from images once they discovered they had been generated by AI.

H&M said it worked with real models in 2025 to make "digital representations/twins of the models" who "themselves retained full control and ownership of their digital twin".

However this "exploration was paused during spring 2025" to consider the next steps.

Balmain, Levi's, TikTok, Meta and Google were contacted for comment.

articles.body: Conservatives are praising The Killers frontman Brandon Flowers and his new album, "Thrasher," which leans into country western elements and religion. Flowers is best known as the lead singer of The Killers, who achieved global fame in the mid-2000s following the release of their multi-platinum debut album, "Hot Fuss," which featured hits like "Mr. Brightside." Flowers, a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, has drawn cultural attention with an album centered on Americana, family, and a spiritual yearning for God amid a troubled world. "Two things can be true at the same time. The fact that I love new wave and rock and roll has been well documented. But a life is long enough to allow for more. Walt Whitman said it best, ‘I am large. I contain multitudes,’" Flowers said in a trailer for the album. The promotional footage features him driving a classic convertible on a desert highway interspersed with shots of truck stops, diners, ranches, and American flags. "Well, I'm larger now than I was 20 years ago," he continued. "And I've unlocked a room that feels like it's been waiting for me all along. Country-western music, my father's music. It has offered itself to me and the stories I have to tell at the moment with a breezy enthusiasm." SKILLET’S JOHN COOPER SAYS CHRISTIANS WHO CALL ROCK MUSIC ‘DEMONIC’ ARE ‘GETTING THE GOSPEL WRONG’ He noted that this album was recorded in Nashville, Tennessee, clarifying that he is not running away from rock music or his old songs, but rather, "found room for more." The album's focal track, "An American Dream," gained traction following a viral broadcast performance on "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon." The song explores Americana and the illusion of fame as a form of fool's gold, juxtaposed with the value of family and salvation. In the lyrics, Flowers sings about being on the open road while yearning for home, feeling a deep nostalgia for a bygone era, and encountering a roadside billboard that asks, "Where would I spend my eternity?" He later described being picked up by Elvis Presley — as he looked in his 1968 comeback tour — driving a Tesla model X and sober. Elvis laughs when asked if fame was worth it, but cries when mentioning his daughter, eventually handing over the keys and saying, "Put it on Jesus." The recurring chorus then finishes off the song, "Gold and silver, God and glitter. Lights that flicker on hubcap chrome. On the road to Heaven. In Strauss and Stetson. Swimming pools of horsepower. Take me back home." SINGER ZACH TOP SLAMS MODERN COUNTRY MUSIC, SAYS IT LACKS 'SOUL' The release arrives amid a broader, well-documented resurgence of country-western culture, spearheaded by stars like Ella Langley topping the charts. National Review contributing editor Daniel Foster talked about the song as one built on a rough American nostalgia. "The tune itself is great. A hook precision-engineered for bar sing-alongs and a lyric full of James Ellroy, Cormac McCarthy-level American arcana and myth (‘Strauss and Stetson,’ ‘an ad for the Red Man,’ and Elvis Presley in ‘jet-black ’68 comeback leather’)," he wrote. "It’s also fully, unapologetically a song about God — a distinctively American, distinctively American West God, which makes sense since Flowers’s God is Jesus Christ of the Latter-Day Saints." CCM Magazine, a Christian music news outlet, also wrote an extensive review of the album. While he is of a different Christian denomination, Logan Sekulow of CCM Magazine credited Flowers for his frequent references to biblical concepts and images. "[M]arketed ‘Christian’ artists should take note, that Thrasher and the catalogue of Flowers/The Killers contain more direct references to Christ, heaven and biblical principles than you will find on many releases marketed specifically to Christian audiences outside of Worship music," he wrote. "This is the same songwriter who warned about a devil who doesn’t resemble Jesus in 'When You Were Young,' celebrated the sustaining power and rarity of a loving marriage in 'Dying Breed', and retold the emotional arc of the prodigal son in 'Fire in Bone.' Flowers has never treated faith like a decorative accessory. It is part of the architecture of his songwriting." HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER SPENT 25 YEARS PRAYING FOR TINSELTOWN, SAYS 'YOU CAN'T HATE THEM' He specifically praised the use of Elvis as a figure tied to worldly fame and yet yearning for God. "The King becomes something closer to a spiritual predecessor: another larger-than-life performer raised in church, caught between the sacred and the spectacular, now passing something down to the artist who followed him," Sekulow wrote. He then concluded, "The record reaches its destination in a great collision of ‘Gold and Silver, God and Glitter.’ That phrase could almost serve as a mission statement for Brandon Flowers’ Thrasher. Faith and fame, eternity and entertainment, heaven and hell, Las Vegas and Utah. It all finally makes sense when Elvis is there to throw him the keys as he offers one final word to his protégé: ‘put it on Jesus.’" Fox News Digital spoke to conservative culture critic Christian Toto, who called Flowers' performance of the song on "The Tonight Show," "Remarkable. Real. Raw. Passionate. Spiritual. Mesmerizing. Here's a veteran singer who seems to have a new lease on life." He also offered a suggestion as to why country music appears to be having a revival in recent years. "It's more stripped down than other music genres. We have some mighty talents at work at the moment, singers who connect with large, energetic groups of Americans. Morgan Wallen rushes to mind, a singer so popular he survived one of the nastiest, and most unfair, Cancel Culture attacks and only grew bigger," he said. "It's a genre that allows for God, for love, for spirituality, and for a hunger to touch dirty, get dirty and get back up again. With A.I. looming, and smart phones keeping us digitized, there's a greater need for something soulful and true." articles.title: Conservatives pledge to scrap £100,000 childcare 'cliff edge'
articles.summary: Party leader Kemi Badenoch tells the BBC that she wants to see "people who work harder" not getting punished for doing so.
articles.body:
The Conservatives have promised to scrap the "absurd cliff edge" that mean parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Under the current system, only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for government-funded or tax-free childcare.

"What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so," Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

The party said the move would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest.

This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday.

Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare for children aged between nine months and four years old.

However, to qualify both parents must earn less than £100,000 a year.

The same £100,000 threshold applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme .

For every £8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds £2, up to £2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare.

The Tories said they would remove the £100,000 threshold entirely so parents no longer lose childcare support when their income exceeds this level.

The threshold has been criticised by economists, who point out it can leave parents worse off overall even after a pay rise of tens of thousands of pounds.

Badenoch told the BBC the party didn't want "people to stop working because of that".

Speaking before the party's conference, she added: "What we want to see is more people in work and not taking the wrong decisions or the wrong choices, and it doesn't matter whether they're earning £10,000 or £100,000 - what matters is that people are out there working".

Asked if this could result in someone who earns £1 million a year get free childcare under a Conservative government, Badenoch responded: "It doesn't matter what you earn - we don't want you to be punished for working hard. What we're trying to do is grow our economy."

The Tories argue the threshold may mean some people may delay having children until their incomes change, or decide not to start a family at all, describing scrapping it as "both pro-family and pro-growth".

By providing an increased incentive to work, the Tories said the move would also boost economic growth.

They added that it would tackle the "unfairness" that the threshold is calculated on an individual earner's income rather then for the whole household.

In a statement, Griffith said: "Removing this childcare cliff edge is the first step in our mission to deliver lower, simpler, and fairer taxes across the board."

The party said the policy would be funded by cutting the number of public servants working in "executive non-departmental public bodies" - organisations which have a role in the processes of national government but operate at arm's length from ministers, such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.

It said this would save £1.6bn by 2029-30, covering the estimated £700 million cost of removing the childcare "cliff edge".

Badenoch arrived in Birmingham on Saturday ahead of the annual conference, and vowed the party was new and different from the one that lost the 2024 general election.

The party - which is currently polling behind Labour and Reform UK - is expected to use the event to lay out more of its growing policy agenda ahead of the next general election.
